abstract.p: To develop a rehabilitation resilience scale (RRS) for caregivers of children with cerebral palsy (CP) and to examine its reliability and validity. This study was conducted in three phases. Phase I involved item development through a literature review and semi-structured interviews, followed by Delphi expert consultations. In phase II, a pilot survey was conducted with 50 caregivers to evaluate item clarity, comprehensibility, and acceptability. Phase III involved a large-scale psychometric evaluation with 436 participants, including item selection and analyses of validity and reliability. Two rounds of Delphi consultation yielded strong expert agreement. The final scale comprised 47 items across seven dimensions. Psychometric testing demonstrated a content validity index of 0.973. Exploratory factor analysis showed a 7-factor structure, accounting for 70.139% of the total variance. Confirmatory factor analysis further supported the robustness of the 7-factor, 47-item structure. The overall Cronbach’s α of the scale was 0.952, with the dimension-level Cronbach’s α values ranging from 0.837 to 0.947. The test–retest reliability was 0.866 (4-week-interval). The 47-item RRS demonstrates robust psychometric properties and represents a reliable and valid instrument for assessing rehabilitation resilience among caregivers of children with CP.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Cerebral palsy (CP) is a group of permanent disorders of movement and posture caused by non-progressive disturbances in the developing brain. Epidemiological data on CP indicate a global prevalence ranging from 0.20% to 0.30%1. CP remains the leading cause of childhood disability worldwide and imposes substantial limitations on children’s daily functioning and developmental trajectories2,3. Although multidisciplinary rehabilitation can improve motor and cognitive outcomes, CP has no definitive cure, and long-term management depends primarily on the sustained involvement of family caregivers4,5.

Caring for a child with CP presents enduring psychological, physical, and social challenges. Compared with caregivers of typically developing children, caregivers of children with CP often experience substantially higher levels of stress, emotional distress, and caregiving burden6. This may reduce their participation in rehabilitation activities and adversely influence children’s therapeutic outcomes7.

Resilience has been recognized as a key protective factor that enables individuals or families to maintain or regain functioning when faced with adversity8. However, existing resilience frameworks and measurement tools were developed primarily for general populations or adult caregiving contexts and may not fully capture the unique, task-specific demands of caring for a child undergoing long-term rehabilitation9. General resilience refers to an individual’s broad adaptive capacity in response to diverse life stressors, while family resilience focuses on how family systems collectively mobilize resources to cope with challenges10,11. In contrast, rehabilitation resilience is a context-specific construct that reflects the dynamic adaptive processes demonstrated by caregivers specifically within the prolonged, task-intensive environment of pediatric rehabilitation. It encompasses the psychological, behavioral, and resource-mobilizing capacities that enable caregivers to sustain rehabilitation responsibilities despite continuous stressors.

Despite its relevance, no validated instrument currently exists to assess resilience within this rehabilitation-specific context for caregivers of children with CP. Using general or family resilience scales may obscure essential caregiving-related processes and yield inaccurate or incomplete assessments. To address this gap, the present study aims to develop and validate the rehabilitation resilience scale (RRS), a psychometrically robust instrument designed specifically to measure the resilience of caregivers engaged in the rehabilitation of children with CP. Establishing such a tool is essential for accurately identifying caregivers at risk of poor adaptation, tailoring supportive interventions, and ultimately enhancing rehabilitation outcomes for children.

sec.title: Developing the preliminary item pool
sec.p: The initial item pool of the RRS for caregivers of children with CP was generated through a comprehensive synthesis of systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials focusing on resilience measurement or caregiving in CP. A systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed, Ovid, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, EMBASE, WANFANG DATA, and CNKI. Medical subject headings (MeSH) terms and keywords included “cerebral palsy,” “caregiver,” “resilience,” “scale,” and “assessment.” The search covered publications from database inception to March 2021.

sec.title: Semi-structured interviews
sec.p: To ensure that the scale adequately reflected caregivers’ experiences, semi-structured interviews were conducted with five caregivers of children with CP receiving rehabilitation services at the Affiliated Hospitals of Putian University. Purposeful sampling was used to achieve variation in caregiver age, caregiving duration, and rehabilitation experience. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. The interview guide (Online Appendix A), informed by existing literature, explored emotional, contextual, and behavioral factors influencing rehabilitation resilience. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analyzed using the qualitative content analysis framework proposed by Elo and Kyngäs12. The emergent categories were integrated with findings from the literature review to refine and expand the preliminary item pool.

sec.title: Delphi expert consultation
sec.p: A two-round Delphi process was undertaken to evaluate item relevance, clarity, and conceptual alignment. Sixteen experts in physiotherapy, pediatric medicine, pediatric nursing, rehabilitation nursing, and scale development were recruited using targeted sampling to ensure both disciplinary diversity and representativeness. All experts had at least 10 years of relevant professional experience, consistent with methodological recommendations for Delphi studies13,14. Experts rated each item using a 5-point importance scale (from “very important” to “very unimportant”) and provided qualitative feedback. Consensus indicators included the mean importance score, coefficient of variation (CV), full-score ratio, and Kendall’s W. Item retention criteria followed established Delphi guidelines, including mean importance score ≥ 3.5, full-score ratio ≥ 0.20 and CV ≤ 0.2515.

sec.title: Phase II: pilot testing
sec.p: A pilot survey was conducted with 50 caregivers to evaluate item clarity, comprehensibility, and acceptability. A sample size of 30–50 participants was considered adequate for pilot testing to identify issues related to item wording and response processes16. Participants were recruited using convenience sampling from a provincial tertiary rehabilitation hospital in Fujian Province, China, in October 2021. Inclusion criteria for children with CP were: (1) aged ≤ 14 years and (2) receipt of continuous or intermittent rehabilitation training. Children with comorbid conditions such as asthma, epilepsy, malignant tumors, or other chronic diseases were excluded. Inclusion criteria for caregivers of children with CP were: (1) aged ≥ 18 years; (2) serving as the child’s primary caregiver for more than 8 h per day; (3) being a family member of the child, and (4) willingness to participate in the survey. Caregivers with mental or communication disorders or those receiving financial compensation for their caregiving services were excluded. For participants with limited literacy, the researcher read each item aloud and recorded responses accurately. A 5-point Likert scale (from “strongly irrelevant” to “strongly relevant”) was used to assess item comprehensibility. All participant feedback was systematically reviewed.

sec.title: Participants and sample size
sec.p: A cross-sectional survey was conducted from January to May 2022 at two tertiary hospitals in Fujian Province using the Wen Juan Xing online platform (https://www.wjx.cn). Inclusion and exclusion criteria were consistent with those employed in the pilot study. For multivariate psychometric analyses, a sample size of 5–10 participants per item was recommended17. Given that the initial scale consisted of 57 items and allowing for an estimated 20% rate of invalid responses, a minimum sample size of 342 participants was deemed sufficient.

list-item.p: General information questionnaire: A self-developed questionnaire was used to collect demographic and clinical information on both children and their caregivers, including the child’s age, gender, and rehabilitation status, as well as the caregiver’s age, gender, education level, occupation, and monthly family income.

Connor-Davidson resilience scale (CD-RISC): The CD-RISC was selected as the criterion measure of general psychological resilience. The validated Chinese version demonstrated strong psychometric properties (Cronbach’s α = 0.91)18. The scale comprises 25 items across five dimensions (competence, instinct, tolerance of negative affect, control, and spiritual influences) rated on a 5-point Likert scale. Total scores ranging from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating higher levels of resilience.

Initial RRS for caregivers of children with CP: The initial scale consists of 57 items across seven dimensions: acquisition of knowledge or skills (9items), pursuit of rehabilitation goals (8 items), family support (8 items), friend support (9 items), healthcare provider support (8 items), emotional management (8 items), and assumption of caregiving responsibilities (7 items). Items were rated on a 5-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (“strongly disagree”) to 5 (“strongly agree”). Total scores of the initial RRS range from 57 to 285, with higher scores indicating higher levels of rehabilitation resilience.

sec.title: Item selection
sec.p: Statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS 26.0 software. Dispersion, discrimination, and correlation coefficient analyses were adopted for item selection to assess the sensitivity, representativeness, and discriminability of the scale items. Item dispersion was evaluated by calculating the CV, with items having a CV value < 15% being removed15. A discrimination analysis was conducted by comparing the top 27% high-scoring group with the bottom 27% low-scoring group based on the total scale score, and items with a critical ratio (CR) < 3 or P > 0.05 were removed19. The correlation coefficient was used to calculate the correlation between the score of each item and the total score of the scale, with items having a correlation coefficient < 0.4 or P > 0.05 being removed20.

list-item.p: Content validity: The content validity index of the scale (S-CVI) and the item-level (I-CVI) for each item were assessed based on ratings provided by experts21. A CVI > 0.80 was considered evidence of “excellent” content validity22.

Construct validity: A combination of exploratory factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was utilized to determine the scale’s construct. EFA was performed on half of the sample (odd-numbered cases), with the Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin (KMO) test performed23. Principal component analysis was utilized to extract common factors with eigenvalues > 1, followed by factor rotation to interpret the factor structure. Items were removed based on the following criteria24–26: factor loading < 0.4; factor loading ≥ 0.4 on two or more factors; fewer than three items per common factor; factors not aligning with the scree test. EFA verified whether the number of extracted common factors matched the originally constructed dimensions. CFA was conducted on the remaining sample using AMOS 24.0 software to assess model fit. Acceptable fit indices included a chi-square to degrees of freedom ratio (x2/df) < 3, root mean square residual (RMR) < 0.05, incremental fit index (IFI) > 0.9, comparative fit index (CFI) > 0.9, and Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) < 0.05, with 0.05 ≤ RMSEA ≤ 0.08 indicating a reasonable model24,27.
Criterion-related validity: The correlation between the CD-RISC and the RRS was calculated. A correlation coefficient (r) > 0.7 indicates high validity of the study’s scale28.

Known-groups validity: Known-groups validity was assessed by comparing RRS scores across caregiver and child subgroups with theoretically expected differences (e.g., caregiver education, child functional status). Prior literature indicates that resilience varies according to socioeconomic factors and caregiving burden, providing conceptual justification for the selection of these groups29. Statistical significance was set at P < 0.05.
Cronbach’s α coefficient: Internal consistency reliability was evaluated using Cronbach’s α with values > 0.8 indicating good reliability24,30.

Test–retest reliability: Four weeks after the survey with a sample size of 10–15% of the total sample31, 50 caregivers were retested using purposeful sampling, and the correlation coefficient (r) was calculated. An r > 0.70 indicated good stability of the scale32.

sec.title: Ethical approval
sec.p: This study obtained approval from the Ethics Committee of the Affiliated Hospitals of Putian University, China, with approval number: PYFL [202215]. Prior to their enrollment in the study, all participants were comprehensively informed about the study’s objectives, potential benefits and risks, as well as the measures in place to safeguard the confidentiality of their personal information. Participants were also informed that their participation was entirely voluntary and that they possessed the right to either engage in or withdraw from the study at any stage during the research process, without any negative consequences. Informed consent was obtained from each participant before their involvement in the study.

sec.title: Item generation
sec.p: The literature review and semi-structured interviews with caregivers yielded an initial pool of 55 items, covering seven dimensions: Acquisition of knowledge or skills, Goal Achievement, Family Support, Friend Support, Healthcare Provider Support, Emotional Management, and Assumption of Caregiving Responsibility.

sec.title: Delphi expert consultation
sec.p: Sixteen experts in physiotherapy, pediatric medicine, rehabilitation nursing, pediatric nursing, and scale development from eight provinces in China completed two rounds of Delphi consultation (response rate: 100%). The expert authority coefficient (Cr) was 0.86, and Kendall’s W increased from 0.117 in Round 1 to 0.264 in Round 2 (both P < 0.05), indicating a significant improvement in expert consensus. Based on expert feedback after Round 1, the names of two dimensions were revised: “Acquisition of Knowledge or Skills” was revised to “Acquisition and Application of Knowledge or Skills,” and “Goal achievement” was revised to “Pursuit of Rehabilitation Goals.” Seven items were deleted, including two items with CV values > 0.25 and others due to low importance ratings or qualitative expert feedback. Four semantically overlapping items were merged into two, and 14 new items were added, resulting in a revised item pool of 60 items. After Round 2, three additional items were removed, including one with a CV values > 0.25, one with a full-score ratio < 0.20, and one based on the expert feedback. The Delphi process concluded with a 57-item pretest version, reflecting strong expert consensus on item relevance and clarity.

sec.title: Phase II: pilot testing
sec.p: A total of 50 questionnaires were distributed and subsequently collected, yielding a response rate of 100%. All items were reported by participants to be clear and understandable. Following group discussions, the research team decided to temporarily retain all items from the pilot testing. The 57-item version was used for psychometric testing.

sec.p:

sec.title: Item selection
sec.p: All 57 items met statistical criteria for retention. The analysis revealed the CV ranging from 0.191 to 0.338 for each item. Discrimination analysis showed the CR ranging from 7.708 to 19.689 for all items (all P < 0.001). The correlation between the total score and each item ranged from 0.452 to 0.745 (all P < 0.001). Given the satisfactory results in discrimination and relevance, no items were removed at this stage.

list-item.p: Content validity: Content validity was assessed using data from the second round of Delphi consultation. The I-CVI values ranged from 0.750 to 1.000, and the S-CVI was 0.973, with dimension-level S-CVI values ranging from 0.938 to 0.986. These results indicate excellent agreement among experts.

Exploratory factor analysis: The KMO value was 0.911, and Bartlett’s test was significant (χ2 = 10,217.500, P < 0.001), indicating suitability for factor analysis. In the first EFA, eight factors with eigenvalues greater than 1 were extracted, accounting for 69.249% of the total variance. Communalities of the 57 items ranged from 0.349 to 0.857. Ten items were subsequently removed due to low loadings, cross-loadings, or weak factor structure. The scree plot showed that eigenvalues plateaued after the eighth factor (Fig. 1), suggesting that extracting seven factors for varimax rotation was appropriate. A second EFA conducted on the remaining 47 items yielded a stable 7-factor structure, explaining 70.139% of the total variance. Communalities of the 47 items ranged from 0.455 to 0.829, and all factor loadings exceeded 0.40. This factor structure was consistent with the originally proposed conceptual framework, demonstrating strong explanatory power for rehabilitation resilience among caregivers of children with CP. Detailed factor loadings were provided in Supplementary Tables S1and S2.

Confirmatory factor analysis: CFA supported the adequacy of the 7-factor, 47-item structure. The model demonstrated good fit: χ2/df = 1.82, RMR = 0.041, IFI = 0.905, CFI = 0.905, RMSEA = 0.063, with all indices meeting recommended thresholds (Table 2). Standardized factor loadings ranged from 0.46 to 0.89, indicating satisfactory convergent validity (Fig. 2).

Criterion-related validity: The total score of RRS demonstrated a strong correlation with the CD-RISC total score (r = 0.733, P < 0.001). Correlations between the seven RRS dimensions and the CD-RISC total score ranged from 0.487 to 0.612 (all P < 0.001), supporting good convergent validity of the RRS (Table 3).

Known-groups validity: The RRS total scores showed significant differences across caregiver age, relationship to the child, place of residence, educational level, marital status, and monthly family income (all P < 0.05; Table 4). These findings were consistent with the theoretical expectations that socioeconomic and familial factors influence caregiver resilience, thereby supporting the known-groups validity of the RRS.

sec.title: Reliability analysis
sec.p: The final 47-item scale demonstrated excellent reliability. The overall Cronbach’s α was 0.952, with values for the seven dimensions ranging from 0.837 to 0.947. Test–retest reliability (4-week interval) yielded a coefficient of 0.866 for the total scale and ranged from 0.781 to 0.884 across dimensions (all P < 0.01), indicating good stability.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study developed and validated the RRS for caregivers of children with CP, addressing the absence of a psychometrically sound instrument specifically designed to assess resilience within the context of long-term pediatric rehabilitation caregiving. The scale was developed following established psychometric procedures, incorporating a literature review, qualitative interviews, Delphi expert consultations, and statistical validation.

Two rounds of Delphi consultation involving 16 multidisciplinary experts yielded strong consensus and excellent content validity. Item refinement was conducted based on expert feedback to improve both scientific rigor and clinical relevance. Subsequent psychometric evaluation in a caregiver sample demonstrated that the RRS possesses sound measurement properties, supporting its potential utility for both research and clinical practice.

Several resilience-related scales have previously been developed, including the family resilience assessment scale10, family hardiness index33, and family strength index34. However, these scales primarily assess general family functioning or stress-coping capacity rather than resilience in the context of long-term caregiving and rehabilitation. Although general resilience scales such as the Connor-Davidson resilience scale (CD-RISC) have been widely used and demonstrated good psychometric properties across populations35, their broad conceptual scope may limit sensitivity to the unique demands experienced by caregivers of children with CP. In contrast, the RRS was explicitly designed to capture rehabilitation-specific adaptive processes, integrating both individual and contextual dimensions of caregiving resilience36–38.

The final RRS encompasses seven dimensions: (1) acquisition and application of knowledge or skills, (2) pursuit of rehabilitation goals, (3) family support, (4) friend support, (5) healthcare provider support, (6) emotional management, and (7) assumption of care responsibility. this multidimensional structure reflects contemporary resilience frameworks that conceptualize resilience as a dynamic process arising from interactions between individual capacities and environmental resources. For instance, the prominence of the Acquisition and Application of Knowledge or Skills, as well as Pursuit of Rehabilitation Goals dimensions highlighted the central role of sustained therapeutic engagement in CP rehabilitation. Recent advances in telerehabilitation and teleassessment have increased caregiver involvement in treatment delivery and monitoring39–41, which may further reinforce the importance of rehabilitation skills and self-efficacy within caregivers’ resilience profiles. In addition, social support emerged in three distinct subdomains (family, friends, and healthcare providers), highlighting differentiated sources of external resources within caregivers’ resilience systems. This differentiation may reflect sociocultural characteristics of caregiving in Asian contexts, where family-centered responsibility, peer support from other caregivers, and professional guidance from healthcare providers each play distinct and complementary roles. The Emotional Management and Assumption of Care Responsibility dimensions capture internal regulation and role adaptation, both of which are essential for sustaining long-term engagement with demanding rehabilitation regimens. The scale’s structure thus aligns with contemporary resilience models, which emphasize dynamic interactions between individual capacity, social support, and contextual demands36–38.

From a clinical perspective, the RRS offers several potential applications. First, its domain-specific structure allows clinicians to identify caregivers’ strengths and vulnerabilities, thereby facilitating individualized support strategies. For example, high scores in support-related domains may reflect existing relational resources, whereas lower scores in knowledge acquisition or emotional management may indicate a need for targeted education, psychological support, or structured home-based interventions. Second, the RRS may serve as a useful tool for monitoring changes in caregiver resilience over time, particularly in settings where remote assessment and digital rehabilitation platforms are increasingly incorporated into CP management42. Finally, the scale may serve as an outcome measure in trials evaluating caregiver-focused or family-centered rehabilitation interventions, such as structured home programs41 or digital monitoring systems.

sec.title: Limitations and future directions
sec.p: Despite its strengths, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the Delphi panel was selected using purposive sampling rather than random selection, which may limit the generalizability of expert consensus. Second, participants in the psychometric evaluation were recruited from two tertiary hospitals within a single province in China; thus, findings may not fully represent caregivers from diverse cultural, socioeconomic, or healthcare contexts. Future studies should aim to (1) validate the RRS across diverse geographic and cultural settings; (2) examine its sensitivity to change in longitudinal and intervention-based studies; (3) explore measurement invariance across caregiver subgroups (e.g., mothers vs. fathers); and (4) assess the utility of the RRS within digital or hybrid rehabilitation models, aligned with the growing global emphasis on teleassessment and telerehabilitation42.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The RRS is a psychometrically sound, multidimensional scale developed to assess resilience among caregivers of children with CP. The scale demonstrates excellent content validity, a stable seven-factor structure, and strong internal consistency and test–retest reliability. Further validation in larger, more diverse, and cross-cultural populations is warranted to strengthen its generalizability and ultimately enhance its utility in guiding tailored, caregiver-centered interventions.
